764.title: the dice game
764.hook: Duryodhana walks through Maya's hall, mistakes floor for water and water for floor, and hears laughter
764.howItsDone: Some Hindu storytellers treat Duryodhana's humiliation in Maya's hall as the opening of the dice-game story, the small wound that leads to the great quarrel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shishupala's light rose and entered Krishna, and the Rajasuya was finished. Your line was where you'd rather turn that light. Did you notice where your attention went? Day seven hundred sixty-four.

The guests have gone home. But one guest has stayed behind. Duryodhana lingers at Indraprastha with his uncle Shakuni, wandering through the great hall the asura builder Maya made for the Pandavas. It's a hall of wonders, and wonders can be tricky. Floors that look like water. Water that looks like floor. Doors that seem open and aren't. A new story starts here, and it's called the dice game. But it doesn't start with dice. It starts with a man walking through a beautiful room and getting it wrong, again and again.
screen: `ONE GUEST STAYS BEHIND.` → `MAYA'S HALL OF WONDERS.` → `IT STARTS WITHOUT DICE.`

segments.voice: In the telling, Duryodhana comes to a spot on the floor that looks like a pool. It's crystal, but he takes it for water, and he gathers up his clothes to wade across. Nothing wet. Then he comes to a real pool, so clear it looks like solid floor, and he walks straight in, clothes and all. And here's the line that hurts: Bhima sees it, and laughs. The servants laugh too. Yudhishthira, the host, sends him dry clothes. It doesn't help. A little further on, Duryodhana tries to walk through a doorway that looks open, and strikes his head on a wall of crystal. At another door, which really is open, he holds back, thinking it closed. By the end of his visit, the hall has fooled him over and over, and his mistakes have had an audience. Hold onto what happened here, because it's small, and it's going to be enormous. Nobody attacked Duryodhana. Nobody planned this. A beautiful building and a little laughter. But he has just watched kings from near and far bring gifts to his cousin, and now his cousin's house has made him look like a fool. The poem is careful here. It doesn't excuse him for what comes next. It just shows us the moment the wound opens. The dice game, when it comes, will look like a game of chance. But its roots are here, in a man walking alone through a room that made him feel small, with laughter behind him.

If you pray, you can remember them kindly in your prayer. If not, simply wish them ease. The bell holds the time.
Dyuta, the game of dice this story is named for. A story that doesn't begin with dice, but with Duryodhana fooled by Maya's hall, and laughed at as he falls.
Your line: help before you laugh. Today, when someone slips up in front of you, help before you laugh. Day seven hundred sixty-four.

765.title: the dice game
765.hook: on the road home, Duryodhana tells Shakuni what is eating him, and Shakuni offers a way to win without a war
765.carry: name the sting before it becomes a plan
765.howItsDone: In Hindu retellings of the Mahabharata, Shakuni is known as the master of the dice, and the conversation on the road is told as the moment Duryodhana's envy becomes a plan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dice game began without dice: Duryodhana fooled by Maya's hall, and laughed at. Did you help before you laughed? Day seven hundred sixty-five.

Duryodhana is heading home to Hastinapura, and he keeps sighing. His uncle Shakuni, riding with him, notices and asks what's wrong. And Duryodhana tells him. Not a polite version. The whole thing. In the poem, he pours it out: the kings bowing to his cousin, the wealth flowing in, the hall that made a fool of him, the laughter. He says he can't bear it. He says it's burning him up inside. Today, a confession on the road, and the uncle who hears in it an opportunity.
screen: `SIGHING ON THE ROAD HOME.` → `SHAKUNI ASKS.` → `THE WHOLE THING POURS OUT.`

segments.voice: Listen to what Duryodhana actually says. He doesn't say the Pandavas cheated. He doesn't say they wronged him. He says they're prospering, and he can't stand it. Their success is the injury. That's envy in its plainest form, and the poem lets him say it out loud, without dressing it up. Shakuni listens. Then he does what a good friend might do, at first. He tells Duryodhana not to grieve, that the Pandavas have their good fortune and he has his. But Duryodhana won't be comforted. So Shakuni changes course. You can't beat them in battle, he says, in effect. They're too strong. But there's another way. Yudhishthira loves to play dice, and he doesn't play well. I do. Invite him to a game, and I'll win everything he has, and you won't have to lift a weapon. Sit with how clever that is, and how dark. A war would be open. Everyone would see who attacked whom. A game is different. It looks friendly. It has rules. The loser agreed to play. Shakuni is offering Duryodhana a way to take a kingdom and keep his hands clean. And notice who starts this. Not a monster from a cartoon. A hurting man, and an uncle who knows exactly where it hurts. The dice game is born on this road, out of envy spoken aloud and a plan offered in reply.

766.title: the dice game
766.hook: Duryodhana and Shakuni work on the blind king, a hall is built for the game, and Vidura's warning goes unheeded
766.carry: let a worry change one thing
766.howItsDone: In Hindu retellings, Vidura is remembered as a voice of wise counsel at the Kuru court, the one who tells the blind king what he doesn't want to hear.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dice game was born on the road: Duryodhana's envy, and Shakuni's plan to win without a war. Your line was name the sting before it becomes a plan. Did you name a sting before it became a plan? Day seven hundred sixty-six.

A plan needs permission. Duryodhana is a prince, not the king. To invite Yudhishthira to anything, the invitation has to come from his father, Dhritarashtra, the blind king of Hastinapura. So uncle and nephew go to the palace. Shakuni speaks first, gently, about how pale and thin the prince has grown. And the king, who loves his son, asks him what's wrong. Today the plan moves from a road to a throne room, and we watch a father decide.
screen: `A PLAN NEEDS PERMISSION.` → `TO THE BLIND KING.` → `A FATHER ASKS WHAT'S WRONG.`

segments.voice: Duryodhana tells his father what he told Shakuni: the Pandavas' wealth, the kings at their feet, the hall that shamed him. And Shakuni lays out the game. Dhritarashtra hesitates. In the telling, he says he wants to ask Vidura first, his wise half-brother, whose counsel he trusts. And Duryodhana pushes back hard. If you ask Vidura, he says, in effect, Vidura will stop it, and I'll be lost. He presses until his father gives way. So the king orders a new hall built for the game, a splendid one, worthy of the guests. Only then does he call Vidura, not to ask whether, but to tell him. And Vidura says plainly that he doesn't approve. This game, he warns, will set the cousins against each other. It will end in quarrel. Dhritarashtra listens, and doesn't change course. He answers that if the gods are kind, no harm will come; that what is fated will happen. And then he gives Vidura a job. Go to Indraprastha, he tells him. Bring Yudhishthira here to play. Look at what's happened. The one man who sees the danger clearly is the one sent to deliver the invitation. A father who couldn't say no to his son has made the counselor he trusts most the messenger of the thing he warned against. The poem doesn't call Dhritarashtra wicked. It shows a man who heard the warning, and loved his son too much to act on it.

767.title: the dice game
767.hook: before the first throw, Yudhishthira calls the game deceit, Shakuni dares him, and he plays anyway
767.howItsDone: The dice scene is retold in homes, on stage and on screen, and the talk before the first throw is a place where readers and listeners stop to argue about Yudhishthira's choice.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the dice game, the blind king had a hall built, and sent Vidura, who had warned against it, to carry the invitation. Your line was let a worry change one thing. Did you let someone's worry change one thing before you went ahead? Day seven hundred sixty-seven.

Vidura has delivered the invitation, and Yudhishthira has come. The new hall is ready. The guests are seated, the cloth is spread, and the dice are out. Before anyone throws, there's a conversation, and it's easy to hurry past it on the way to the drama. Don't. Everything that follows is already folded inside it. Yudhishthira says plainly what he thinks of this kind of game. Shakuni answers him, and the answer has a hook in it. And a choice gets made in the open, before the elders have even taken their seats. Today, the talk before the first throw.
screen: `THE BOARD IS SET.` → `A CONVERSATION FIRST.` → `A CHOICE MADE IN THE OPEN.`

segments.voice: In the telling, Shakuni opens. The hall is full, he says; it's time to play. Yudhishthira doesn't pretend. He says that gambling of this kind is deceit, that there's no warrior's courage in it, and he asks Shakuni not to beat them by crooked means. Shakuni has an answer ready, and it's clever. Every contest, he says, is one person knowing more than another. A skilled player beats an unskilled one, a learned person beats one who isn't, and nobody calls that cheating. Then the sting: if you're afraid, don't play. Yudhishthira's reply is the hinge of the whole episode. Called to play, he says, I don't turn back; that's my vow. And he adds that fate rules everyone. So he asks who he'll be playing against. Duryodhana answers: I'll put up the wealth, and my uncle Shakuni will throw for me. Yudhishthira sees the problem at once. One man playing with another's stake, he says, seems to him against the rules. But if that's how they want it, let it begin. Look at what happened in those few lines. He named the danger. He named the unfairness. He was told, nearly in so many words, that refusing would look like fear. And he walked forward anyway, holding a vow and a belief about fate. Some readers call that integrity. Others call it pride. The poem gives both of them something to hold. The elders come in and take their seats, Bhishma, Drona, Kripa and Vidura among them, the poem says with heavy hearts. Yudhishthira puts down his first stake, a costly pearl set in gold. Shakuni throws. And he wins.

768.title: the dice game
768.hook: stake after stake, the same short line: I have won; and Vidura warns that the winner is in danger too
768.howItsDone: Vidura's warnings in the dice hall are a place where teachers and storytellers often pause, and his image of the honey-gatherer is retold as a picture of desire that can't see its own danger.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the dice game, the talk before the first throw: a warning, a dare, a vow, and a pearl set in gold lost. Your line was ask whose voice that is. Did you catch yourself saying you couldn't back down? Day seven hundred sixty-eight.
screen: `CALLED TO PLAY, I DON'T TURN BACK.`

segments.voice: There's a line in this part of the poem that keeps coming back, like a drumbeat. Yudhishthira names a stake. Shakuni throws. And then Shakuni says, in effect: I have won. Then again. And again. The poem repeats it until the words themselves begin to sound like a warning. Today we sit inside that drumbeat, and we listen to the one man in the hall who stands up and tries to stop it.
screen: `A LINE LIKE A DRUMBEAT.` → `I HAVE WON.` → `ONE MAN TRIES TO STOP IT.`

segments.voice: After the pearl, Yudhishthira reaches for the next stake. Treasure. Gold. A fine chariot. Servants. Elephants. Horses. Soldiers. Each time he describes what he's putting down, carefully, almost proudly, as if the quality of the stake could change the fall of the dice. Each time, the throw goes to Shakuni, and the same short sentence follows: I have won. Notice what that refrain does. It takes the suspense away. We stop asking who will win the throw. We start asking something harder: why doesn't he stop? Somebody in the hall asks it out loud. Vidura, the blind king's wise half-brother, turns to Dhritarashtra. In the telling, he gives him a picture. A man climbs high after honey, and he's so taken with the honey that he doesn't see the fall in front of him. That, Vidura says, is your son with the dice. He begs the king to stop the game while there's still a family left to save. Duryodhana answers Vidura with scorn. He accuses him of always speaking for the other side, against the very family that shelters him. And Dhritarashtra says nothing that stops the game. Here's what's striking. Vidura's honey picture isn't about Yudhishthira, the one losing. It's about Duryodhana, the one winning. In the poem's eyes, the winner is in danger too. Each throw won for him is a step nearer the edge, and he can't see it, because his hands are full of honey.

769.title: the dice game
769.hook: the brothers staked one by one, Yudhishthira himself, and then Draupadi
769.carry: name it plainly, the way he did
769.howItsDone: The last stakes of the dice game are read aloud and staged as a turning point of the epic.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the dice game, the drumbeat of I have won, and Vidura's man reaching for honey. Did you look for the edge of a streak? Day seven hundred sixty-nine.

Every treasure is gone. In the telling, Yudhishthira stakes his herds, his lands, his city, even the ornaments the princes wear. Lost, every one. And then the game changes from a matter of things to a matter of people. Shakuni asks, is there anything left? There is. Sitting near Yudhishthira, listening to all of it, are his four brothers. Today, the last stakes of the dice game, and the moment the hall is shaken.
screen: `EVERY TREASURE IS GONE.` → `IS THERE ANYTHING LEFT?` → `HIS FOUR BROTHERS.`

segments.voice: Yudhishthira stakes Nakula, one of the twins. Shakuni throws, and wins. He stakes the other twin, Sahadeva. Lost. Then Shakuni tries something sly. The twins, he says, are Madri's sons. Surely Bhima and Arjuna, Kunti's sons, your own mother's sons, are dearer to you. You won't stake them. It's an attempt to split the brothers along their mothers' line. And Yudhishthira, losing everything, still catches it. He says, in effect: you're trying to divide us, and that's wrong. Then, as if to show they can't be divided, he stakes Arjuna. Lost. He stakes Bhima. Lost. He stakes himself. Lost. Shakuni says there's still one stake left: Draupadi. And Yudhishthira stakes her, describing her goodness as he does. Now the poem turns to the room. The elders, Bhishma, Drona and Kripa, are shaken; the telling says they break into a sweat. Vidura holds his head in his hands. The blind king, who can't see the board, keeps asking whether the throw has been won. Shakuni throws. And he wins. Look at the strange shape of that last streak. Yudhishthira's loyalty to his brothers is real. He refuses to let Shakuni set them against each other. And that same loyalty is what he puts on the board, one brother after another. A virtue and a disaster in the same breath. The stakes run out here, with a woman lost in a game she never sat down to play. What she does next turns the hall upside down.

770.title: Draupadi's question
770.hook: a messenger walks to Draupadi's door and comes back carrying a question: whom did you lose first?
770.carry: whom did you lose first, yourself or me
770.howItsDone: Draupadi's question is retold in homes, dance and theater, and it's discussed by readers and commentators as a question about dharma and law that the epic leaves open.

segments.voice: Yesterday the last stakes of the dice game fell: the twins, Arjuna, Bhima, Yudhishthira himself, and then Draupadi. This week ran from Duryodhana's stumble in Maya's hall to the last stake in the dice hall. Your line was name it plainly, the way he did. Which moment from the whole week stays with you? Day seven hundred seventy.

The game is over, and Duryodhana wants Draupadi brought into the hall. First he tells Vidura to fetch her. Vidura refuses flatly. In the telling, he says she can't have become anyone's slave, because Yudhishthira staked her after he'd already lost himself. Hold on to that. It's the thread of everything that follows. Duryodhana turns instead to an usher, a servant whose job is carrying messages, and sends him to the women's rooms. Today, a messenger walks to Draupadi's door, and walks back carrying a question.
screen: `VIDURA REFUSES TO FETCH HER.` → `HE LOST HIMSELF FIRST.` → `A MESSENGER AT HER DOOR.`

segments.voice: The usher tells Draupadi what has happened: Yudhishthira, carried away by the game, has lost her to Duryodhana, and she must come. Draupadi doesn't come. She asks him to go back and put one thing to the gambler in the hall: whom did you lose first, yourself or me? It's a precise question. If he lost himself first, he was no longer free when he staked her, and perhaps had nothing left to stake. If he staked her first, the answer is different. She isn't pleading. She's asking for the facts the whole claim rests on. The usher carries it back and asks it in the hall. And Yudhishthira says nothing. The telling says he sits as if he's lost his senses, and answers not a word, good or bad. Duryodhana tells the usher: let her come here and ask it herself. The usher goes back, uneasy, and Draupadi sends him again. This time her question isn't only for Yudhishthira. Ask the assembly, she says, what is right for me to do, and I'll do it. Watch how the question grows. First it was for one man. Now it's for a whole hall of kings and elders. The usher, caught between a furious prince and a woman who won't be moved, hesitates to go a third time. So Duryodhana sends his brother Duhshasana instead. The messenger stage is over. And the question, still unanswered, is about to walk into the hall in person.
screen: `THE USHER: YOU'VE BEEN LOST.` · `WHOM DID YOU LOSE FIRST?` · `YUDHISHTHIRA SAYS NOTHING.` · `ASK THE WHOLE ASSEMBLY.` · then, large: `THE QUESTION GROWS.`

segments.voice: Let the breath slow, and the hands rest open. Bring to mind a question you've been wanting to ask but haven't: about a decision made for you, or something that didn't add up. Don't answer it. Just let it take shape, as plainly as Draupadi's did. Who decided? On what grounds? Hold your question gently, and breathe with it. If you pray, you can bring it into your prayer. If not, let it sit with you in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Draupadi's question. Sent back with a messenger: whom did you lose first, yourself or me? Then sent to the whole hall.
Your line: whom did you lose first, yourself or me. Today, when a decision lands on you, ask one plain question about how it was made. Day seven hundred seventy.
